entities.description: The opposite time courses A and B cause the reversal effect. Depending on the time course over which a real event is viewed, a positive event becomes a negative one, and vice versa. Dominant expectation turns into manifest reality. Core principle of the theory.

The anticipation of future events that can be consciously controlled by the individual. It acts as an active top-down vector on the generative external reality and can trigger the reversal effect if dominant. Expectation actively generated through attention and thinking, which can be specifically changed and controlled and thereby has a direct influence on perception and action. An active cognitive act in which the individual anticipates a goal or event in the future. In the model, it acts as a vector that potentially has a top-down effect on shaping reality.

The strongest active expectation within a system that largely determines the resulting reality or perception and overrides other expectations. A firmly anchored belief in the future that overrides other expectations and shapes perception and action.
Expectation about the future that becomes dominant due to intensity or isolation. Triggers direct reversal effect.

Basic rule to protect against catastrophic reversal effects: Do not form dominant expectations of the future, instead act in the now and feel joy. Further specification: Not the absence of positive expectations for the future, but the avoidance of free, fully agreed and identity-bound expectations of a specific future outcome. Modeling and background hopes are permitted as long as they are kept as hypotheses and allow for external testing.

The aggregated directional belief of the majority of market participants about future price developments. When this expectation becomes dominant – i.e. h. when almost all visible analysts, media and private investors agree on the same view - it becomes a self-destructive force. Beckmann logic identifies this condition as a primary prerequisite for a reversal effect in markets.

Preconception cementation is the active or passive process by which a system protects its existing preconceptions from refutation - even in the face of external scrutiny to the contrary. It differs from simple error in that it structurally deactivates the system's ability to learn: it is not the pre-assumption that is adapted to reality, but rather the interpretation of reality that is adapted to the pre-assumption. According to Beckmann logic: The system becomes 'blind' - it loses the ability to distinguish between positive and negative results.

A quantitative measure that expresses the proportion of active expectations in a system that are focused on a single dominant outcome compared to all other competing outcomes. When this ratio exceeds a critical level - indicating near-complete expectation convergence - the system enters a pre-reversal state. The relationship formalizes what has previously only been described qualitatively as dominant expectation dominance.

An index that measures the degree to which available cognitive or social resources for forming new expectations have been consumed by a prevailing expectation. High saturation indicates that no corrective expectation can form organically, making the system brittle. It operationalizes the structural condition under which reversal becomes not only possible but structurally inevitable once a triggering event occurs.

The temporal developmental path of an individual agent's expectations from initial formation through reinforcement, dominance and finally contradiction. Mapping the trajectory shows the sub-phases of the consolidation of expectations that build up to the crossing of the threshold. A steep, uninterrupted trajectory toward a single prevailing expectation results in a sharper reversal than a trajectory that contains intervening corrective signals.

A self-reinforcing social dynamic in which the expression of the dominant expectation by each actor increases the perceived legitimacy and strength of that expectation for all other actors and further suppresses alternatives. The cascade operates under conscious consideration and is driven by pressures for conformity, signals of authority, and the availability of confirmatory information. It is the primary mechanism through which preconceptions are consolidated at the collective level.

The level of active cognitive processing demands placed on a person at the precise moment when incoming information contradicts the prevailing expectation. High cognitive load at threshold prevents the person from engaging in corrective reappraisal, making reversal more likely and severe. Low cognitive load allows partial recalibration before the contradiction fully triggers the reversal sequence.

A formal model that specifies the quantitative limit at which expectation dominance in a system transitions from stable anticipation to the reversal-triggering region. It integrates dominance ratio, saturation index and temporal persistence to produce a threshold that can be monitored in advance. Without this model, the safety principle can only react to a completed reversal, but cannot prevent it from detecting the crossing point before it occurs.

The identifiable phase immediately before the threshold is exceeded, in which the dominance ratio and the saturation index have reached critical values, but no triggering event has yet occurred. In this phase, external signals of disconfirmation are systematically filtered or reinterpreted to maintain the prevailing expectation rather than correcting it. This phase is the final actionable intervention window in which the safety principle can be applied preemptively to break the cascade before a reversal becomes structurally inevitable.

The phenomenon whereby a single cognitive distortion in a thought system becomes so strong that it overwhelms all other sources of information and completely controls perception. Corresponds to the principle of dominant expectation in the knowledge graph on the individual psychological level: An assumption occupies the entire perception system and makes correction signals invisible.

A threshold range after which a system state changes to another state abruptly or with difficulty in reversing. For Beckmann logic, the tipping point is the physical form of a long-prepared reversal event.
Social pressure not to openly doubt a shared expectation. It makes dominance visible because opposing positions become risky not only in terms of content but also socially.

An external event or information signal whose significance and clarity exceeds the collective reversal threshold of a group or institution and initiates a rapid transition from dominant expectation to expectation seeking. Social tipping point triggers differ from ordinary, disconfirmatory signals in that they cannot be integrated into the existing prevailing expectation - they represent such a large prediction error that the collective simulation must be abandoned. Their effectiveness depends on their public visibility, their resistance to narrative reframing, and the current level of calibration of dominant group expectations.

A self-reinforcing configuration in which a common dominant expectation becomes the dominant cognitive framework of an entire group and divergent expectations are suppressed through social pressure and assimilation. The pattern arises when individual prevailing expectations are synchronized between members, creating a collective simulation that treats the shared prediction as an established reality rather than a probabilistic forecast. Threshold effects determine when enough individual expectations have converged to stabilize the dominant expectation at the group level against reversal signals.

A stable state in which an institution has committed resources, personnel, and reputational capital to a prevailing expectation so extensively that the expected costs of expectation revision exceed the expected costs of maintaining the dominant prediction, even in the face of conflicting signals. Institutional lock-in differs from ordinary expectation persistence in that it is structurally maintained by prior decisions rather than ongoing evidence, creating a simulation in which reversal triggering signals are interpreted as noise rather than prediction errors. Lock-in dynamics are the institutional analogue of the calcification of individual dominant expectations.

A group-level analogue of the individual security principle, in which a collective maintains institutional practices and norms that limit excessive commitment to prevailing expectations, preserve channels for divergent predictions, and schedule regular external reality tests. The collective security posture operationalizes the security principle at the institutional level: instead of individual presence and noncommitment, structural provisions such as protection of minority opinions, mandatory adversarial review, and scenario planning are required that prevent full integration of group simulation into the prevailing expectation. Groups with a strong collective security posture have lower collective reversal thresholds, allowing for an earlier correction before lock-in.

A feedback mechanism by which group members suppress their private expectancy signals in favor of the dominant group expectation, thereby reinforcing the apparent strength of that expectation and delaying the onset of collective reversal. This mechanism uses social pressure to conform as a reversal amplifier: every individual who gives up his minority expectation reinforces the prediction of the dominant group, increases the calibration value of the dominant expectation and makes institutional corrections increasingly difficult. The mechanism is strongest when group membership and identity are at stake.

The holographic universe according to Leonard Susskind. A theoretical physical model that states that the information of a volume in the universe is encoded on its surface. This enables macroscopic physics to be described as a holographic projection.
A scaling error in the spatial representation (floating point precision error) at extremely large distances.

entities.id: Dark matter in the brain model
entities.description: A dynamic gravity correction factor that ensures the stability of galaxies at low matter densities.

Capacity limit – The limit of biological information processing. Since the brain cannot calculate the entire complexity of the quantum world, it uses heuristics, shortcuts and simplifications (such as solid matter or linear time).

A local system collapse (singularity) due to an 'arithmetic overflow'. The gravity and density values exceed the representable numerical range of the space-time grid, which leads to the deletion of the local coordinate structure.

entities.id: Quantum field theory and vacuum fluctuation
entities.description: Quantum field theory and vacuum fluctuation – basis of the Standard Model: Fields are fundamental, particles are excitations. Even the vacuum has zero point energy and fluctuations (Casimir effect). According to this picture, the outside world is not an empty space, but a fluctuating quantum field continuum.

Loop Quantum Gravity – Quantization of spacetime itself: Space consists of discrete spin networks with minimal area/volume. No extra dimensions necessary. Also without experimental confirmation, it competes with string theory to explain the origin of quantum mechanics.

String theory – hypothesis that fundamental constituents are not point particles but rather one-dimensional oscillating strings. Mathematically elegantly unifies quantum mechanics and gravity, but has not yet provided a testable prediction. Serves as an alternative rendering principle for the data source in the main graph.

Origin of quantum mechanics – meta question: Why is the outside world quantum and not classical? Is quantum logic fundamental or does it emerge from a deeper information-based reality? Affects the question of whether the human logic model experiences the quantum rules as a limit to its rendering ability.
The principle that all phenomena within the simulation must be explained by the simulation's own rules and data.
The 4D rendering grid of the simulation.
The hard-coded parameters of the simulation (e.g. gravitational constant, speed of light) that ensure a stable macroscopic representation.

The only valid confirmation that a problem has been truly addressed (and not just the symptoms) is external reality, not internal judgment. The test: Has the generative mechanism that caused the problem been changed? If the same problem could occur again under similar conditions, the solution would be stabilization and not a solution. This external review must be performed explicitly after each troubleshooting cycle. Internal consensus that a problem is “solved” is a weak test; The observable change in system behavior under real conditions is the meaningful test.
Attraction describes the tendency of systems to converge towards one another with increased information exchange or compatible states (physically, biologically or socially interpretable).

fundamental cause. Explanation: In the current model of physics, a gas nebula has a high entropy due to disorder and a black hole has a very low entropy due to maximum order. Attraction here is not an increase in entropy. The logic model described here, on the other hand, assumes a view of reality that is based on the TSVF (two-state vector formalism). The past remains here, just as the future already exists. The total entropy in this model is composed of the matter distribution, which is minimal in a black hole, and the information exchange, which is maximum in a black hole. In this model, the entropy resulting from the exchange of information is absolutely dominant in a black hole.
weak effect
Gravity factor in the collision area is less than 1, as in gas nebulae

entities.id: Gravity at the edge of the galaxy
entities.description: Gravity factor greater than 1

Gravity factor in the entire, diffuse galaxy equals 1, since there is no different distribution of matter. Explanation: Diffuse galaxies without measurable dark matter, such as NGC 1052-DF2 and NGC 1052-DF4, are extremely rare, obscure galaxies that challenge the common model of galaxy formation. These ultra-diffuse dwarf galaxies, about 65 million light-years away, are composed almost entirely of stars and gas, without the expected dark matter halo. The graph mentions NGC 1052-DF2 as a galaxy without dark matter (factor 1). This is an excellent touchstone! If the distribution of matter there is so uniform that no information gradient arises, this confirms the theory. This point should be considered a “zero calibration” on the graph.
Gravity factor less than 1

Own hypothesis as an information-theoretical interpretation of a linear global potential (γ r) discussed since Mannheim & Kazanas 1989. Approach: G(new) = G(standard) * Gf(ρ,T) with ρ = baryonic density, T = information transparency as a measure for coherent information exchange (not yet operationally quantified, hence qualitative hypothesis). T would be high in empty space/low density with coherent exchange and low in diffuse, scattering media such as gas nebulae. Qualitative regimes derived from this as falsifiable predictions: Gf>1 in the outer edge of galaxies (explains rotation curves without halo), Gf<1 in gas nebulae and collision zones of colliding galaxies (explains apparent absence of DM there), Gf=1 in homogeneous diffuse galaxies such as NGC1052-DF2 as zero-point calibration without information gradient. Formal anchor: Mannheim-Kazanas metric B(r)=1-2β/r+γr-kr², γ term as global contribution of the rest of the universe. Status: Qualitative hypothesis bordering on open question, as long as T is not quantitatively formalized.
The increase in information is a decisive effect

In this area, the classical theory of gravity is expanded by an information-theoretical model based on the two-state vector formalism (TSVF). The fundamental interaction occurs through the exchange of gauge bosons (such as photons for magnetism or hypothetical gravitons for gravity), which act as quantum information carriers between state vectors. The special feature of this model lies in the gravity factor Gf(ρ,T): Information transparency (T): In an “empty space” the transparency for the flow of information between the vectors is high, which strengthens the effective attraction in the edge region of galaxies (Gf>1). Information noise: A “highly filled room” or “diffuse informants” (such as gas mist) generate noise, which hinders signal transmission and lowers the gravity factor (Gf<1). The increase in entropy is primarily defined here by the flow of information, which reaches its maximum in extremely compact objects such as black holes despite a high level of material order, since the exchange between past and future (according to TSVF) absolutely dominates here. The “zero point calibration” on diffuse galaxies without dark matter (e.g. NGC 1052-DF2) proves that the standard gravity (Gf=1) applies without information gradients.

The hypothesis that axions or axion-like particles form dark matter. The QCD axion was originally proposed to solve the Strong CP problem of quantum chromodynamics and can also represent a dark matter component. Axions are among the most important candidates that continue to be investigated experimentally.

Experimental strategy searching for rare interactions of a dark matter candidate with a detector material. Experiments use, among other things, large amounts of xenon, argon or other sensitive detector materials. To date, no generally accepted direct evidence of a dark matter particle has been achieved.

The cosmological phenomenon of the accelerated expansion of the universe. It denotes an observed property of cosmic expansion rather than a specific identified form of matter. In the standard model of cosmology, this phenomenon is described by a cosmological constant or vacuum energy density, whose fundamental physical nature is not clear.

entities.id: Dark matter as a form of matter
entities.description: The hypothesis that the dark matter phenomenon is caused by a previously unidentified form of matter that is gravitationally effective but interacts electromagnetically only very weakly or not at all. In the Standard Model of cosmology, such a non-baryonic component of matter is described as cold dark matter. The existence of a concrete microscopic form of matter has not yet been directly proven.

The astrophysical and cosmological phenomenon that observed gravitational effects and the development of cosmic structures cannot be fully explained by directly observable baryonic matter alone. The evidence includes, among other things, galaxy dynamics, galaxy clusters, gravitational lensing, the cosmic microwave background radiation and large-scale structure formation. This empirical discrepancy must be distinguished from the assumption that its cause is a concrete new form of matter.

The large-scale distribution of dark matter around galaxies assumed in the standard model of cosmology. The halo extends well beyond the visible stellar galaxy and provides an additional gravitational mass component, which serves, among other things, to explain the observed rotation curves of galaxies and other dynamic effects.

entities.id: Emergent gravity according to Erik Verlinde
entities.description: A theoretical approach by Erik Verlinde in which gravity is not seen as a fundamental interaction, but as an emergent phenomenon of a deeper description of space-time, information and microscopic degrees of freedom. In certain regimes, the approach can generate additional gravitational effects that are phenomenologically reminiscent of dark matter or MOND. The theory does not represent an experimentally confirmed identification of dark matter as a form of matter.

entities.id: Gravitational lensing evidence for dark matter
entities.description: The observation of gravitational lensing effects, the strength and spatial distribution of which cannot be fully explained by the observed baryonic matter. Gravitational lensing allows the gravitational mass distribution to be reconstructed regardless of whether the matter in question is electromagnetically visible, and therefore provides important evidence for the dark matter phenomenon.

The totality of the theoretically proposed microscopic particles or fields that could form dark matter as a form of matter. The candidates include WIMPs, axions, axion-like particles, sterile neutrinos, ultralight bosons and particles from so-called hidden sectors. So far, no candidate has been clearly identified as dark matter.

The current standard model of cosmology. It describes the universe through, among other things, ordinary baryonic matter, cold dark matter and a dark energy component, which in the simplest model is represented by the cosmological constant lambda. Lambda-CDM explains a large number of independent cosmological observations with a common model, without clarifying the microscopic nature of dark matter or dark energy.

The open question of which physical entity is responsible for the dark matter phenomenon. In particular, it is unclear whether the cause is a new particle or field component, complex dark sector physics, a modification of gravity or another previously unknown physical structure. The astrophysical evidence for the phenomenon is strong, while its microscopic cause remains unknown.

Modified Newtonian Dynamics, an alternative theory or a phenomenological approach, according to which the dynamics at extremely small accelerations deviate from Newtonian dynamics. MOND was developed specifically to explain the rotation curves of galaxies and can describe many galactic observations without a dark matter halo. However, the transfer to a complete relativistic and cosmological theory remains problematic.

The observation that the orbital velocities of stars and gas in many spiral galaxies do not decrease as sharply at large radii as would be expected from the visible baryonic matter distribution and classical gravity. The phenomenon is important evidence for the dark matter phenomenon, but can also serve as motivation for modified gravitational theories such as MOND.

entities.id: Difference between dark matter and dark energy
entities.description: The conceptual and physical distinction between two different cosmological phenomena. The dark matter phenomenon refers to additional gravitational effects that can be attributed to a missing mass component or, alternatively, to a change in gravity. The dark energy phenomenon, on the other hand, refers to the accelerated expansion of the universe. Dark matter and dark energy are therefore neither the same physical entity nor two manifestations of the same observed phenomenon.

The hypothesis that dark matter consists of weakly interacting massive particles. WIMPs have long been a leading candidate due to their expected weak interactions, their possible thermal formation in the early universe, and their natural embeddedness in various extensions of the Standard Model. Despite extensive direct, indirect and collision-based searches, no WIMP has yet been clearly detected.

entities.id: Illustrative model for the phenomenon dark energy
entities.description:
Model: Space as an observer-dependent construct

The traditional view of dark energy can be replaced by an alternative image that is not based on a physical force, but on the nature of human space perception.

The starting point: the flat paper
Consider a piece of paper lying flat on a stable surface. On small and medium scales this paper appears perfectly flat. This corresponds to the scientific observation that space has a flat geometry locally and at measurable distances.

The phenomenon: curvature on large scales
However, when looking at extremely large scales, the perception changes. An image of a leaf can be drawn whose distant edges appear to be bent upwards. However, this deviation from flatness is not a physical property of a 'spatial structure' and is not caused by an external energy source.

The cause: the observer effect
Rather, it is purely an observer effect. Similar to how relativistic effects (time dilation or length contraction) occur when approaching the speed of light, the perception of space changes when observing extreme distances. Space is not understood as a fundamental element of the universe, but rather as a model constructed by the human brain for processing information.

Conclusion
The observed expansion, usually attributed to dark energy, is in this model an artifact of human space construction. What is interpreted as physical expansion is the result of a perspective distortion that occurs as soon as the observer exceeds the limits of locally flat perception.

entities.id: Dark energy (as a mysterious form of energy)
entities.type: hypothetical form of energy, not found
entities.description: Dark energy as a form of energy is what scientists suspect. It's just an unproven hypothesis.
The phenomenon of dark energy is what scientists are observing. It's real.

Dynamic change of spatial structures depending on information density and energy distribution (e.g. expansion or local distortion). However, spatial expansion could only appear to be present. The spatial expansion is then an observer-dependent construction that only seems to take place in the observer's model.
black hole as a bubble, not as a singularity

Hannibal's campaign against Rome (218–202 BC) is a unique double case study in the theoretical system: In phase 1 (crossing the Alps, Cannae), Hannibal masterfully exploits Rome's dominant expectations and creates reversal effects in his favor - analogous to Rehhagel's outsider victories. In phase 2 (after Cannae) Hannibal himself falls into attachment to the future ("Rome will capitulate") and thus triggers his own spiral of disappointment - analogous to the failure of the favorites in Rehhagel or the elite in the French Revolution. Rome, on the other hand, carries out an exemplary external examination and analysis of assumptions after Cannae.

Friedrich's potato strategy is a unique case study in the collection: for the first time, the reversal effect is not used passively (by staying outside of dominance), but rather actively used as a tool - by consciously creating an artificial dominance in an out-group (the population), the reversal of which then produces the desired result. The problem was a classic presupposition problem: 'Potatoes are worthless.' The low-complexity solution ('convince the population directly') would have generated resistance. The highly complex solution used the psychological structure of dominance itself as leverage.

This graph analyzes two events under Otto Rehhagel - the championship of 1. FC Kaiserslautern in 1998 and Greece's European Championship victory in 2004 - as application examples for the reversal effect, Beckmann logic and the security principle. Both events follow the same pattern: a non-dominant expectation (outsider) meets a dominant expectation of the opponents and the public. Through presence, tactical discipline and questioning of preconceptions, the reversal effect is actively used instead of feared.

This graph encodes a structural insight that results from comparing all previous historical graphs: the reversal effect does not have a fixed time scale. It operates at the level of hours (Cannae), weeks (Rehhagel), decades (Attic Sea Confederation, French Revolution) and centuries (Potato/Ireland). The question is: what determines the timescale? The answer that this theoretical system suggests: the depth of anchoring of the dominant expectation and the speed of feedback that enables correction.

The First World War is the most complex case study in the collection so far because it shows three coupled time scales: (1) Short scale (weeks/months): The dominant expectation of a 'short victory war' fails due to trench warfare. (2) Middle scale (years): The military leadership falls into future attachment ('final victory') and ignores the presence of the soldiers. (3) Long scale (decades): The stab-in-the-back legend constructs a false assumption that, as political dominance, prepares the next catastrophe. This graph is therefore primary evidence for the time scale graph and the pattern of cross-scale coupling.

Preconception cementation refers to the process by which a system – human, institution, AI – actively protects its existing preconceptions from being refuted by external scrutiny. It is the direct counterpart to presupposition analysis (Beckmann logic) and the main mechanism through which external testing becomes ineffective. The paradox: The more firmly an assumption is cemented, the greater the amplitude of the later reversal effect - and the longer the time scale until reversal. Cementation is therefore not only a problem of knowledge, but also a catastrophe amplifier.
This knowledge graph describes the path to superintelligence development based on a theory of expectation and future reality. It is intended as a first draft and invites optimization.

A strategy that always seems to be the best choice, regardless of the behavior of all other actors. It arises from a dominant expectation about the behavior of others and cements itself because deviant behavior appears irrational. Formal equivalent of the dominant expectation at the strategy level.

State in which the expectations of all actors about the behavior of others are correct and the actual strategies confirm these expectations. The concept makes explicit what Nash equilibria epistemically presuppose: a system of coordinated dominant expectations that stabilizes itself.

Nash equilibrium that is stable against the entry of actors with different strategies. Corresponds to a dominant collective expectation that is so deeply anchored that deviations are systemically punished. Combines game theory with evolutionary logic and shows how dominant expectations are stabilized biologically and culturally.

Prototypical game structure in which two actors achieve a collectively suboptimal Nash equilibrium through simultaneous dominant strategies. Both expect the other to defect and therefore defect themselves - even though mutual cooperation would be better for both. Demonstrates how dominant expectations about the behavior of others create a systemic reversal effect.

The problem of which Nash equilibrium among several possible ones is reached when actors align their expectations about each other's behavior. Shared dominant expectations (Focal Points according to Schelling) act as a coordination mechanism. Shows how unconscious collective expectations constitute game-theoretical realities.

Repeated games in which players learn from previous rounds and adjust their expectations about others' future behavior. Cooperation arises from the expectation of future interaction. Corresponds to the learning principle of the graph: Historical experience modifies dominant expectations for future situations.

Situation in which actors have multiple Nash equilibria and the outcome depends on which expectations prevail about the behavior of others. No dominant strategy exists; the result is determined by shared or divergent structures of expectations. Shows that expectations are not just reactions, but actively shape reality.

entities.id: Market expectation as a Nash equilibrium
entities.description: Financial market prices as a Nash equilibrium of aggregated expectation strategies: If the majority of market participants have the same dominant expectation, the system converges into an equilibrium that becomes unstable due to the reversal effect. Consensus trading as a dominant strategy trap: The consensus itself destroys the expected result.

State in a strategic game in which no player can gain an advantage by unilaterally changing his strategy. Everyone involved has adjusted and fixed their expectations to one another. Corresponds to a state of collective dominant expectations that stabilize each other and create or permanently prevent a reversal effect at the system level.

The paradox that individually rational behavior produces collectively irrational results. Each actor follows his dominant expectation and dominant strategy — the collective outcome is worse for everyone. Formal correspondence of the reversal effect at the level of social systems: Individual expectation rationality produces collective reality reversal.

A natural focal point that actors converge on without explicit communication because it is considered obvious or prominent. Schelling points arise from shared expectation structures — dominant unconscious expectations that all actors share. Shows how collective unconscious expectations pre-structure game theory equilibria.

Game-theoretical interpretation of the security principle: Instead of fixing a dominant strategy (which leads to the suboptimal Nash equilibrium), an actor acts according to the minimax-regret principle — he minimizes the worst possible outcome without forming a dominant expectation about the system's behavior. This corresponds to 'acting without expectation' in formal language.

The game theory reformulation of the reversal effect: If all actors simultaneously fix their dominant expectations about the system's behavior and act accordingly, they collectively produce exactly the opposite result of their individual expectations. The Nash equilibrium they reach is the formal model of the systemic reversal effect.

Robust strategy in repeated games: Start with cooperation, then react in a mirrored manner to the opponent's last behavior. Does not force equilibrium through dominant expectation, but rather through reciprocal adjustment. Formal counterpart to the security principle: acting in the now without fixed expectations of the future, but with situational responsiveness.

The cognitive tendency to base judgments and decisions disproportionately on an initial reference value (the anchor), even if this is irrelevant or arbitrary. In the context of Beckmann logic: The anchor is often the initial dominant expectation that distorts all subsequent evaluations.

The reinforcement of a belief or behavior simply by the fact that it is already widespread. The bandwagon effect is the mechanism by which an initially random dominant expectation becomes a market expectation or social belief—a direct precursor to market reversal events.

The tendency to preferentially seek out, interpret, and remember information that confirms an existing belief. Acts as a self-reinforcer of dominant expectations: the stronger an expectation, the more selective the information intake - and the more difficult it is to correct before the reversal effect.

The tendency of groups to place pressure for conformity over critical thinking and to suppress dissent. Groupthink creates collective confirmation bias at the group level: the dominant expectation of the group is no longer questioned by anyone until the reversal effect occurs.

The phenomenon that individuals align their behavior and beliefs with the perceived majority opinion, regardless of their own information. Herd behavior transforms individual cognitive biases into collective dominant expectations — it is the social amplification mechanism of the reverse effect.

The psychological state of tension that arises when new information conflicts with existing beliefs or expectations. Cognitive dissonance is the moment in which the reversal effect first becomes noticeable - and at the same time the moment in which the dominant cognitive distortion fights most strongly against correction.

The ability to construct mental scenarios that deviate from actual reality ('What if...?'). Serves as a cognitive tool against dominant expectations: Anyone who actively plays through alternative scenarios loosens the cognitive fixation on a single image of the future and reduces the probability of the reversal effect.

The systematic overestimation of one's own ability to judge and predict. Actors with high self-overestimation develop particularly strong dominant expectations and underestimate the probability of the reversal effect because they consider their model of reality to be more reliable than it is.

A structured method for preventing errors in advance: You assume that a project has failed and analyze in retrospect what could have gone wrong. Effective counterbalance to overconfidence and dominant expectations as it forcefully activates counterfactual thinking and makes the reversal effect visible before it occurs.

The unconscious filter through which the brain only perceives and processes those environmental stimuli that are compatible with existing expectations and schemas. Selective perception is the fundamental mechanism that enables all other perceptual distortions and explains the persistence of dominant expectations.

The irrational tendency to incorporate irretrievable investments (time, money, energy) that have already been made into future decisions. In relation to Beckmann logic: The sunk effort reinforces the dominant expectation of the original plan and prevents the process-oriented action that the security principle demands.

The tendency to judge the likelihood of an event based on how easily a similar example comes to mind. Lively, emotionally charged expectations are thereby systematically overestimated - which promotes the emergence of dominant expectations.

The empirically proven principle that losses are psychologically weighted about twice as much as equivalent gains. Loss aversion reinforces dominant expectations: The expectation of a loss is felt so intensely that actions are taken that trigger the reversal effect - avoiding the loss creates it.
A positive social environment that encourages innovation and lowers the barrier to experimentation with Level 2 and 3 solutions.

The fundamental non-integrability and exponential divergence of trajectories in the classical gravitational three-body problem (PoincarÃ© 1889). Serves as diagnostic evidence that the macroscopic physical model exceeds the computational capacity of the brain.

The depth of the anchoring of a dominant expectation largely determines the time scale of the reversal effect. Anchoring levels (from shallow to deep): (1) situational – tied to a specific encounter (hours); (2) episodic – tied to a competition or campaign (weeks/months); (3) institutional – encoded in structures and rules (years/decades); (4) cultural – anchored in worldviews and narratives (generations); (5) civilizational – invisible as a natural fact (centuries). The deeper the anchoring, the longer the time scale - and the greater the amplitude of the reversal.
The loss of bright reflective surfaces, which absorbs more energy and increases further warming. The node shows how a local physical effect can force a system-wide expectation correction.

A form of action that reduces risks without clinging to a guaranteed good future. It translates the security principle into climate practice: improving robust processes now, without a salvation narrative.

The physical feedback from the system through extreme events, measurement data, crop failures, water stress or infrastructure load. It is the material control that tests expectations not with arguments, but with real consequences.
The assumption that a system is safe because the expected negative feedback is not yet visible. This all-clear is dangerous because it interprets inertia as a refutation and not as a storage effect.

The unspoken assumption that current forms of energy and prosperity can be continued in the long term. It acts as a background filter that slows down external scrutiny and makes short-term convenience seem like realism.

A non-linearly coupled earth and social system in which physical feedback, human expectations and political reactions intertwine with a time delay. The node forms the core of the subgraph because climate is understood here not only as a natural process, but also as a space for expectations and action.

The event in which expectations that have seemed stable for a long time turn into their opposite due to cumulative physical feedback. Expected controllability turns into loss of control, late correction turns into abrupt compulsion to act.

The property that climatic effects only become visible with a time delay, even though their causes are already taking effect. As a result, expectations can appear to be confirmed for a long time before the material counter-reaction becomes apparent.
A process in which deviations are dampened and a system is returned towards stability. The node represents the climatic equivalent of process-oriented self-correction.

The absorption of large amounts of heat by oceans, which simulates stability in the short term and returns stored changes in the long term. The node explains why a seemingly stable present can contain an already charged future.
The release of bound greenhouse gases from thawing soils, whereby what was initially a slow change gains additional momentum. This shows how late feedback can return not neutrally, but reinforcing.

A process in which a change further reinforces its own causes or consequences. In graph logic, this corresponds to a material spiral of disappointment, because late correction builds up ever greater counterforces.

The expectation that future technology will lift the current burden of action. It can promote realistic innovation, but becomes dangerous when it replaces present action and acts as an attachment for the future.
Technical component in AI systems that blocks the formation of dominant future expectations while modeling remains permitted.

The ability of media or institutional actors to determine, through the selection of topics, what a community thinks about - not what it thinks, but what it deals with. Agenda setting creates the thematic basis on which dominant narratives can emerge.

A linguistically encoded pattern of interpretation that becomes so dominant in a community or institution that it renders alternative perspectives invisible. It serves the same function as the dominant expectation in the model: it defines what is considered normal, probable, and possible and insulates against corrections.

The systematic testing of a narrative against external sources of reality that are not controlled by the narrative itself. Presupposition analysis (Beckmann logic, section 4): Seemingly unsolvable problems become solvable by systematically questioning their basic assumptions. It assumes that external testing is accepted and that assumptions can in principle be corrected. Assumption analysis is the desired state; Assumption cementation is the current state when a system comes under pressure. The transition from one to the other is the crucial tipping point.

Predictive processing theory (Karl Friston, Andy Clark) reformulates the question: The brain is not a passive recipient of stimuli, but an active prediction machine that constantly generates hypotheses about the world and updates them through prediction errors. Actions are themselves predictions - the brain predicts the sensory consequences of a movement and executes movements to fulfill the prediction (active inference). In this framework, “will” is the brain's prediction of its own future action, which then triggers that action. This is neither pure determinism (the prediction is not mechanically fixed - it is context-sensitive, value-weighted and changeable through deliberation) nor libertarian freedom (it is completely physical). It is a sophisticated compatibilism based on neuroscience.

entities.id: Free will and the safety principle (nuclear voltage)
entities.type: Core connection to the base graph (synthesis node)
entities.description: The central synthesis of this subgraph with the base graph: The security principle (“Do not form dominant future expectations – act in the now – intrinsic motivation”) implicitly presupposes a subject who is able to adopt a motivating attitude. This is a compatibilist claim of free will: the agent can reshape the causal structure of his or her own decision-making through conscious practice (process orientation, feedback without hope, modeling vs. expectation). This is not libertarian freedom (the practice is physically realized in neural changes), but real source freedom: the agent becomes the source of actions that result from his or her own restructured values. The paradox: Hard determinism would say that this restructuring would always happen; Nevertheless, the Security Principle treats it as a real practice that one can choose. Solution: Compatibilism resolves this tension - the choice to practice the Safety Principle is free will physically realized through neuroplasticity and conscious attention.

The prevailing position in academic philosophy: Free will and determinism are compatible because “free will” should be redefined. A free action is not an action that is not uncaused, but one that is caused by the correct internal process - specifically, by the agent's own desires, values, and considerations, without external coercion or internal dysfunction. Key versions: (1) Classical compatibilism (Hume, Mill): Freedom = acting according to one's own wishes without external pressure. (2) Hierarchical compatibilism (Frankfurt): Freedom = acting on desires that one supports through reflection (second-order desires). (3) Responsiveness to reasons (Fischer & Ravizza): Freedom = the mechanism that causes the action responds appropriately to reasons. Compatibilism upholds moral responsibility and is the basis of most legal systems.

entities.id: Neuroplasticity as the physical basis of compatibilist freedom

This represents the physical mechanism for compatibilist freedom: the agent's considerations, values, and attention causally restructure the very neural substrate from which future decisions emerge. Over time, the agent becomes a different physical system—a system whose causal structure increasingly reflects its reflective values. Meditation studies (Davidson, Lazar): 8 weeks of mindfulness practice measurably change prefrontal-amygdala connectivity. The practice of “acting without expectations” physically rewires the brain’s reward-prediction circuits.
